Bulk RNA-seq – Differential Expression Analysis with edgeR

Brain · Blood · Muscle (GTEx / recount3)

Giacomo Pogliana

2026-10-15

1 · Libraries and data loading

Three tissue datasets are retrieved from the GTEx project via the recount3 interface: frontal cortex (Brain), whole blood (Blood), and skeletal muscle (Muscle). Each dataset is stored as a RangedSummarizedExperiment (RSE) object.

Raw recount3 data stores per-base coverage rather than read counts. transform_counts() converts coverage to integer counts by scaling each base-level value by the average read length, making the data suitable for count-based statistical models such as edgeR.

library(recount3)
library(recount)
library(edgeR)

rse_brain  <- readRDS("rse_brain.RDS")
rse_blood  <- readRDS("rse_blood.RDS")
rse_muscle <- readRDS("rse_muscle.RDS")

# Convert coverage → counts
assays(rse_brain)$counts  <- transform_counts(rse_brain)
assays(rse_blood)$counts  <- transform_counts(rse_blood)
assays(rse_muscle)$counts <- transform_counts(rse_muscle)

2 · Sample quality control

Before selecting samples for downstream analysis, three QC metrics are inspected for each tissue:

  • RIN (RNA Integrity Number) ≥ 6 — a low RIN indicates RNA degradation, which introduces systematic biases in library preparation and reduces the reliability of expression estimates.
  • Uniquely mapped reads ≥ 80% — a low mapping rate may reflect contamination, poor library quality, or a mismatch between the sample and the reference genome.
  • rRNA fraction < 10% — high ribosomal RNA carry-over suggests incomplete ribo-depletion, which dilutes the mRNA signal and inflates library size without adding informative reads.

These thresholds follow GTEx consortium recommendations and standard bulk RNA-seq best practices.

Brain

# RIN
colData(rse_brain)$gtex.smrin[72:75]
## [1] 5.9 6.8 6.8 6.9
# % mapped
colData(rse_brain)$"recount_qc.star.uniquely_mapped_reads_%_both"[72:75]
## [1] 90.3 88.4 89.1 91.8
# % rRNA
colData(rse_brain)$gtex.smrrnart[72:75]
## [1] 0.1100480 0.0674476 0.0685402 0.0646821

Blood

colData(rse_blood)$gtex.smrin[72:74]
## [1] 7.6 8.6 7.3
colData(rse_blood)$"recount_qc.star.uniquely_mapped_reads_%_both"[72:74]
## [1] 91.7 91.7 89.5
colData(rse_blood)$gtex.smrrnart[72:74]
## [1] 0.00484823 0.00349803 0.00583278

Muscle

colData(rse_muscle)$gtex.smrin[72:75]
## [1] 7.8 8.5 5.7 8.2
colData(rse_muscle)$"recount_qc.star.uniquely_mapped_reads_%_both"[72:75]
## [1] 90.9 89.8 92.0 92.5
colData(rse_muscle)$gtex.smrrnart[72:75]
## [1] 0.00961303 0.00984120 0.00830360 0.01001430

3 · Sample selection and count matrix

Three samples per tissue that pass all QC thresholds are retained, giving a balanced design of 9 samples (3 per group). The count matrices are concatenated column-wise into a single matrix x, and column/row names are assigned for readability.

Using three samples per group is a deliberate trade-off: it satisfies the minimum required for variance estimation in edgeR while keeping the design balanced — a critical requirement for the contrast-based comparisons performed later.

rse_brain_selected  <- rse_brain[,  c(73, 74, 75)]
rse_blood_selected  <- rse_blood[,  c(72, 73, 74)]
rse_muscle_selected <- rse_muscle[, c(72, 73, 75)]

counts_brain_selected  <- assays(rse_brain_selected)$counts
counts_blood_selected  <- assays(rse_blood_selected)$counts
counts_muscle_selected <- assays(rse_muscle_selected)$counts

x <- cbind(counts_brain_selected, counts_blood_selected, counts_muscle_selected)

colnames(x) <- c("Brain73",  "Brain74",  "Brain75",
                 "Blood72",  "Blood73",  "Blood74",
                 "Muscle72", "Muscle73", "Muscle75")

rownames(x) <- rowData(rse_brain_selected)$gene_name

4 · DGEList object

The count matrix is wrapped into a DGEList object, which is edgeR’s core data structure. It bundles counts, library sizes, and sample-level metadata in one place, simplifying downstream function calls.

Alongside the tissue group label, additional QC covariates (RIN, tissue sub-region, sex, age, rRNA fraction, mapping rate, mitochondrial read fraction) are stored in y$samples. These are not included in the statistical model, but are used in the MDS plots (Section 8) to visually assess whether any of them drive unwanted variance.

y <- DGEList(counts = x)

group <- as.factor(c("Brain", "Brain", "Brain",
                     "Blood", "Blood", "Blood",
                     "Muscle", "Muscle", "Muscle"))

y$samples$group <- group

# Quality metadata
y$samples$rin <- as.factor(c(
  colData(rse_brain_selected)$gtex.smrin,
  colData(rse_blood_selected)$gtex.smrin,
  colData(rse_muscle_selected)$gtex.smrin))

y$samples$slice <- as.factor(c(
  colData(rse_brain_selected)$gtex.smtsd,
  colData(rse_blood_selected)$gtex.smtsd,
  colData(rse_muscle_selected)$gtex.smtsd))

y$samples$sex <- as.factor(c(
  colData(rse_brain_selected)$gtex.sex,
  colData(rse_blood_selected)$gtex.sex,
  colData(rse_muscle_selected)$gtex.sex))

y$samples$age <- as.factor(c(
  colData(rse_brain_selected)$gtex.age,
  colData(rse_blood_selected)$gtex.age,
  colData(rse_muscle_selected)$gtex.age))

y$samples$rRNA <- as.factor(c(
  colData(rse_brain_selected)$gtex.smrrnart,
  colData(rse_blood_selected)$gtex.smrrnart,
  colData(rse_muscle_selected)$gtex.smrrnart))

y$samples$mapped <- as.factor(c(
  colData(rse_brain_selected)$"recount_qc.star.uniquely_mapped_reads_%_both",
  colData(rse_blood_selected)$"recount_qc.star.uniquely_mapped_reads_%_both",
  colData(rse_muscle_selected)$"recount_qc.star.uniquely_mapped_reads_%_both"))

y$samples$chrm <- as.factor(c(
  colData(rse_brain_selected)$"recount_qc.aligned_reads%.chrm",
  colData(rse_blood_selected)$"recount_qc.aligned_reads%.chrm",
  colData(rse_muscle_selected)$"recount_qc.aligned_reads%.chrm"))

5 · Low-expression gene filtering

Genes with very low or zero counts across all samples carry no statistical power and inflate the multiple-testing burden. Two complementary checks are applied:

  1. Genes with zero counts in all 9 samples are identified first as a diagnostic step.
  2. filterByExpr() applies edgeR’s recommended filtering strategy: a gene is retained only if it achieves a minimum count (default ~10 reads) in at least as many samples as the smallest group size (here, 3). This threshold is automatically scaled by library size, making it robust across datasets with different sequencing depths.

Setting keep.lib.sizes = FALSE forces recalculation of library sizes after filtering, ensuring accurate normalization factors in the next step.

table(rowSums(y$counts == 0) == 9)
## 
## FALSE  TRUE 
## 38471 15571
keep.exprs <- filterByExpr(y, group = group)
y          <- y[keep.exprs, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]
dim(y)
## [1] 22333     9

6 · TMM normalization

RNA-seq library sizes differ across samples due to technical variation in sequencing depth. Raw counts therefore cannot be directly compared. TMM (Trimmed Mean of M-values) normalization estimates a scaling factor for each sample by computing a weighted trimmed mean of log fold-changes relative to a reference sample, after excluding genes with extreme expression differences (trimming). These scaling factors are stored in y$samples$norm.factors and incorporated automatically into all downstream edgeR calculations.

The boxplots before and after normalization allow a visual check that the distributions are well-aligned after scaling, as expected.

logcpm_before <- cpm(y, log = TRUE)
y             <- normLibSizes(y, method = "TMM")
logcpm_after  <- cpm(y, log = TRUE)

7 · Design matrix

The design matrix encodes the experimental structure that the linear model will fit. The formula ~ 0 + group specifies an intercept-free model where each tissue type gets its own coefficient directly (rather than one group being encoded as the intercept). This parameterization makes it straightforward to define arbitrary contrasts between groups (e.g., Brain − Blood) without algebraic manipulation.

design <- model.matrix(~ 0 + group, data = y$samples)
colnames(design) <- levels(y$samples$group)
design
##          Blood Brain Muscle
## Brain73      0     1      0
## Brain74      0     1      0
## Brain75      0     1      0
## Blood72      1     0      0
## Blood73      1     0      0
## Blood74      1     0      0
## Muscle72     0     0      1
## Muscle73     0     0      1
## Muscle75     0     0      1
## attr(,"assign")
## [1] 1 1 1
## attr(,"contrasts")
## attr(,"contrasts")$group
## [1] "contr.treatment"

8 · MDS plot – exploratory analysis of sample variability

Multi-Dimensional Scaling (MDS) projects samples into a low-dimensional space such that distances approximate the log2 fold-changes between pairs of samples for the top 500 most variable genes (by default). It provides an unsupervised, model-free look at the dominant sources of variance in the data before any formal testing.

Six plots are produced, labelling samples by tissue group and five potential confounders in turn (rRNA fraction, mitochondrial read fraction, age, sex, tissue sub-region). If any confounder label correlates with the spatial separation of samples along a major axis, it should be considered as a covariate in the model.

logcpm <- cpm(y, log = TRUE)

plotMDS(logcpm, col = tissue_cols, labels = group,
        main = "MDS – Tissue")

plotMDS(logcpm, col = tissue_cols, labels = y$samples$rRNA,
        main = "MDS – rRNA fraction")

plotMDS(logcpm, col = tissue_cols, labels = y$samples$chrm,
        main = "MDS – % reads on chrM")

plotMDS(logcpm, col = tissue_cols, labels = y$samples$age,
        main = "MDS – Age")

plotMDS(logcpm, col = tissue_cols, labels = y$samples$sex,
        main = "MDS – Sex")

plotMDS(logcpm, col = tissue_cols, labels = y$samples$slice,
        main = "MDS – Tissue slice")

9 · Dispersion estimation

edgeR models read counts with a Negative Binomial (NB) distribution, which has two parameters: the mean and the dispersion. The dispersion captures gene-to-gene variability in count data beyond what a Poisson model (variance = mean) would predict.

estimateDisp() fits both a common dispersion (shared across all genes) and gene-wise dispersions, shrinking them toward a trended value via empirical Bayes. The BCV (Biological Coefficient of Variation) plot shows the square root of the dispersion estimates: the trend line summarizes how dispersion varies with expression level (highly expressed genes tend to have lower BCV), and the gene-wise estimates scatter around it.

y <- estimateDisp(y, design)
plotBCV(y)

10 · Differential expression – GLM QL F-test

A Quasi-Likelihood (QL) Negative Binomial GLM is fitted to the data. Compared to the standard likelihood ratio test, the QL framework provides a more robust control of type I error, particularly with small sample sizes, by using a gene-level quasi-dispersion estimate that is itself moderated across genes with empirical Bayes.

Three pairwise contrasts are tested:

Contrast Interpretation
(-1, 1, 0) Brain vs Blood (positive logFC = higher in Blood)
(-1, 0, 1) Muscle vs Blood (positive logFC = higher in Muscle)
(0, -1, 1) Muscle vs Brain (positive logFC = higher in Muscle)

The coefficient order follows the alphabetical ordering of the group factor levels: Blood, Brain, Muscle.

fit <- glmQLFit(y, design)

# Brain vs Blood
qlfBLB <- glmQLFTest(fit, contrast = c(-1,  1,  0))
# Muscle vs Blood
qlfMB  <- glmQLFTest(fit, contrast = c(-1,  0,  1))
# Muscle vs Brain
qlfMBL <- glmQLFTest(fit, contrast = c( 0, -1,  1))

Top 10 differentially expressed genes per contrast

Results are ranked by p-value and FDR-corrected with the Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) method, which controls the false discovery rate.

topTags(qlfBLB, n = 10, adjust.method = "BH", sort.by = "PValue")

Saving full results tables

resultsBLB <- topTags(qlfBLB, n = Inf, adjust.method = "BH",
                      sort.by = "PValue", p.value = 1)
resultsMB  <- topTags(qlfMB,  n = Inf, adjust.method = "BH",
                      sort.by = "PValue", p.value = 1)
resultsMBL <- topTags(qlfMBL, n = Inf, adjust.method = "BH",
                      sort.by = "PValue", p.value = 1)

write.table(resultsBLB, "results_Brain_vs_Blood.txt")
write.table(resultsMB,  "results_Muscle_vs_Blood.txt")
write.table(resultsMBL, "results_Muscle_vs_Brain.txt")

DE gene counts at different cut-offs

decideTests() classifies each gene as up-regulated, down-regulated, or not significant under a given FDR threshold and log-fold-change (lfc) cutoff. Comparing results across multiple thresholds (p = 0.05 / 0.01, lfc = 0 / 1) illustrates the sensitivity-specificity trade-off and helps choose a biologically meaningful stringency for downstream analyses.

cat("--- Brain vs Blood ---\n")
## --- Brain vs Blood ---
summary(decideTests(qlfBLB, p.value = 0.05, adjust.method = "BH", lfc = 0))
##        -1*Blood 1*Brain
## Down               5143
## NotSig            11376
## Up                 5814
summary(decideTests(qlfBLB, p.value = 0.05, adjust.method = "BH", lfc = 1))
##        -1*Blood 1*Brain
## Down               4144
## NotSig            13085
## Up                 5104
summary(decideTests(qlfBLB, p.value = 0.01, adjust.method = "BH", lfc = 0))
##        -1*Blood 1*Brain
## Down               3410
## NotSig            14742

11 · Tissue-specific genes

A gene is defined as tissue-specific if it is significantly up-regulated in that tissue relative to both other tissues (FDR < 0.01, logFC > 0). This conservative definition — requiring simultaneous significance in two independent comparisons — reduces false positives that would arise from testing only one pair.

The approach uses set intersection: a gene must appear in the up-regulated set of both pairwise contrasts involving the tissue of interest.

Brain-specific

qlf_BvsBlood  <- glmQLFTest(fit, contrast = c(-1,  1,  0))
qlf_BvsMuscle <- glmQLFTest(fit, contrast = c( 0,  1, -1))

results_BvsBlood  <- topTags(qlf_BvsBlood,  n = Inf)$table
results_BvsMuscle <- topTags(qlf_BvsMuscle, n = Inf)$table

up_BvsBlood  <- rownames(results_BvsBlood[ results_BvsBlood$FDR  < 0.01 & results_BvsBlood$logFC  > 0, ])
up_BvsMuscle <- rownames(results_BvsMuscle[results_BvsMuscle$FDR < 0.01 & results_BvsMuscle$logFC > 0, ])

brain_specific <- intersect(up_BvsBlood, up_BvsMuscle)

Blood-specific

qlf_BloodvsBrain  <- glmQLFTest(fit, contrast = c( 1, -1,  0))
qlf_BloodvsMuscle <- glmQLFTest(fit, contrast = c( 1,  0, -1))

results_BloodvsBrain  <- topTags(qlf_BloodvsBrain,  n = Inf)$table
results_BloodvsMuscle <- topTags(qlf_BloodvsMuscle, n = Inf)$table

up_BloodvsBrain  <- rownames(results_BloodvsBrain[ results_BloodvsBrain$FDR  < 0.01 & results_BloodvsBrain$logFC  > 0, ])
up_BloodvsMuscle <- rownames(results_BloodvsMuscle[results_BloodvsMuscle$FDR < 0.01 & results_BloodvsMuscle$logFC > 0, ])

blood_specific <- intersect(up_BloodvsBrain, up_BloodvsMuscle)

Muscle-specific

qlf_MusclevsBrain <- glmQLFTest(fit, contrast = c( 0, -1,  1))
qlf_MusclevsBlood <- glmQLFTest(fit, contrast = c(-1,  0,  1))

results_MusclevsBrain <- topTags(qlf_MusclevsBrain, n = Inf)$table
results_MusclevsBlood <- topTags(qlf_MusclevsBlood, n = Inf)$table

up_MusclevsBrain <- rownames(results_MusclevsBrain[results_MusclevsBrain$FDR < 0.01 & results_MusclevsBrain$logFC > 0, ])
up_MusclevsBlood <- rownames(results_MusclevsBlood[results_MusclevsBlood$FDR < 0.01 & results_MusclevsBlood$logFC > 0, ])

muscle_specific <- intersect(up_MusclevsBrain, up_MusclevsBlood)

12 · Validation with TPM

To validate the tissue-specificity calls, expression of a representative gene from each tissue-specific list is visualized directly in TPM (Transcripts Per Million) across all samples of all three tissues — using the full RSE objects (not just the 9 selected samples). TPM normalizes for gene length and sequencing depth, making values more interpretable for cross-sample comparisons than raw counts.

A Wilcoxon rank-sum test is used for pairwise comparison because it makes no distributional assumption about the data, which is appropriate given the small sample sizes and the non-normality typical of RNA-seq count data. A significant result (p < 0.05) in both tests confirms that the gene identified as Brain-specific is indeed expressed at consistently higher levels in brain relative to both blood and muscle.

assays(rse_brain)$TPM  <- recount::getTPM(rse_brain)
assays(rse_blood)$TPM  <- recount::getTPM(rse_blood)
assays(rse_muscle)$TPM <- recount::getTPM(rse_muscle)

idx <- which(rowData(rse_brain)$gene_name == brain_specific[1])

boxplot(
  assays(rse_brain)$TPM[idx, ],
  assays(rse_blood)$TPM[idx, ],
  assays(rse_muscle)$TPM[idx, ],
  outline = FALSE,
  names   = c("Brain", "Blood", "Muscle"),
  main    = paste("Expression of", brain_specific[1], "(TPM)"),
  ylab    = "Transcripts Per Million (TPM)",
  col     = c("royalblue", "firebrick", "forestgreen")
)

wilcox.test(assays(rse_brain)$TPM[idx, ], assays(rse_blood)$TPM[idx, ])
## 
##  Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction
## 
## data:  assays(rse_brain)$TPM[idx, ] and assays(rse_blood)$TPM[idx, ]
## W = 4097307, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0
wilcox.test(assays(rse_brain)$TPM[idx, ], assays(rse_muscle)$TPM[idx, ])
## 
##  Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction
## 
## data:  assays(rse_brain)$TPM[idx, ] and assays(rse_muscle)$TPM[idx, ]
## W = 2582195, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

tissue_counts <- sort(tissue_counts, decreasing = TRUE)

13 · Gene list preparation for Enrichr

Tissue-specific gene lists are pre-processed before functional enrichment analysis on Enrichr (https://maayanlab.cloud/Enrichr/). Two filtering steps are applied:

  1. Removal of low-information gene symbols: pseudogenes (LOC), long intergenic non-coding RNAs (LINC), microRNAs (MIR), small nucleolar RNAs (SNORD), and ribosomal protein genes (RPL, RPS) are excluded. These either lack functional annotation in pathway databases or are too constitutively expressed to be informative as tissue markers.
  2. Size cap at 1,500 genes: Enrichr’s statistical tests become less powerful with very large input lists. The top genes by FDR are therefore retained up to a maximum of 1,500.
# Remove poorly informative gene symbols
rm_pattern <- "^LOC|^LINC|^MIR|^SNORD|^RPL|^RPS"

brain_specific_clean  <- brain_specific[ !grepl(rm_pattern, brain_specific)]
muscle_specific_clean <- muscle_specific[!grepl(rm_pattern, muscle_specific)]
blood_specific_clean  <- blood_specific[ !grepl(rm_pattern, blood_specific)]

# Sort by FDR and cap at 1500
ord  <- order(results_BvsBlood[ brain_specific_clean,  "FDR"])
brain_specific_top  <- brain_specific_clean[ord][1:min(1500, length(brain_specific_clean))]

ord2 <- order(results_MusclevsBrain[muscle_specific_clean, "FDR"])
muscle_specific_top <- muscle_specific_clean[ord2][1:min(1500, length(muscle_specific_clean))]

writeLines(brain_specific_top,  "brain_for_enrichr.txt")
writeLines(muscle_specific_top, "muscle_for_enrichr.txt")
writeLines(blood_specific_clean,"blood_for_enrichr.txt")

cat("Brain genes for Enrichr:",  length(brain_specific_top),  "\n")
## Brain genes for Enrichr: 1500
cat("Muscle genes for Enrichr:", length(muscle_specific_top), "\n")
## Muscle genes for Enrichr: 1500
cat("Blood genes for Enrichr:",  length(blood_specific_clean),"\n")
## Blood genes for Enrichr: 1272
